Actionable Steps Toward a Sustainable Energy Future
M8: Renewable Energy Technologies and Innovations
Lesson 1 Overview

Lesson 1 outlines practical, forward-looking strategies to accelerate the global shift toward a sustainable energy future.

It highlights three core areas of action:
Scaling private sector and industrial innovation through strengthened value chains, investment models, and technology co-development;
Investing in workforce development and equitable knowledge sharing.
The lesson emphasizes the importance of inclusive policy design, resilient industrial ecosystems, and collaborative learning—especially across developing economies.
Together, these approaches offer a concrete roadmap to operationalize the energy transition in ways that are just, locally grounded, and globally connected.
M8: Renewable Energy Technologies and Innovations
Part 1: Policy Recommendations for governments
Aligning National Energy Plans with Climate Goals

As major stakeholders, and coordinators in National Energy Plans, governments are the most able to commit to international targets such as NDCs, and make use of policy levers to reach those targets.

A 2025 NDC Partnership report entitled “Tripling Renewables: Powering Climate Action” reveals that, after the first Global Stocktake in 2023 (as mandated by the Paris Agreement), the world is not on track to meet its 2030 obligations.

Getting back on track, and staying on track according to the Global Stocktake, would require a tripling of renewable energy capacity by 2030.

The report notes that 86% of the world’s new power generation capacity in 2023 came from renewable energy, but that deployment is highly concentrated in China, Europe, and the US.

Africa, Southeast Asia, and Latin America collectively accounted for only a fraction of new capacity additions, pointing to regional disparities in policy ambition, financing, and enabling environments.
Furthermore, NDC efforts have been concentrated around the power generation sector, which is usually subject to National Energy Plans that are more ambitious.

Indeed, an IRENA report (IRENA, 2023) finds that G20 countries plan to install 6.3Tw in domestically while pledging 4.6TW in their NDCs, while LDCs and SIDS have aligned their NDCs with their local plans.

This discrepancy highlights the importance of ensuring coherence between national ambitions and international commitments.
As countries prepare their NDC 3.0 submissions, aligning national energy planning with NDCs offers a strategic opportunity to mainstream renewable energy in broader development goals.

Governments should adopt a whole-of-society approach to align energy and climate goals, integrating renewable energy into national development strategies, industrial policies, urban planning, and social protection schemes.
This means convening stakeholders across ministries, utilities, the private sector, civil society, and local communities to ensure that policies are both technically sound and socially equitable.
In addition to strategic planning, regulatory and market-based reforms play a critical role in driving energy innovation and investment.
Forward-looking governments must reform their energy markets to provide long-term signals and incentives for clean energy deployment.
Reforming energy markets to incentivize innovation

Additionally, governments are able to use market signals to incentivize innovation in key sectors, such as energy, which can contribute to accelerating the adoption of renewable energy.

Through carbon pricing mechanisms, governments can send clear market signals that encourage private companies to avoid emission-related costs by investing in cleaner technologies—such as retrofits, carbon capture and storage, and energy efficiency measures—to reduce their carbon footprint.

These signals can be dynamic, as seen in Emissions Trading Schemes (ETS) like the EU-ETS, where registered emitters buy and sell the right to emit greenhouse gases.

This creates a market in which the price of emission allowances is shaped by the limited supply of permits and fluctuating demand, incentivizing companies to reduce emissions cost-effectively.

Carbon emissions can also be priced through a carbon tax, a fixed price per ton emitted.
Carbon taxes provide a constant price signal, allowing firms to plan strategically towards the future.

For ETSs, key considerations include the size and direction of the emissions cap (since a cap that is too high can lead to low allowance prices and weak incentives for innovation) and the volatility of allowance prices.
In contrast, carbon tax schemes benefit from clear and steadily rising price paths, which are more likely to encourage long-term investment and planning by firms.
There exist several options for governments who are looking to reform their energy markets to incentivize innovation and accelerate the adoption of renewable energy.
These include:
Feed-in-tariffs

Feed-in-tariffs allow for renewable energy projects to occur at a larger scale by providing developers with a clear pricing mechanism and predictable source of revenue, removing a key barrier in renewable energy capacity efforts.
Net-metering

Net metering is a billing mechanism that uses a single, bidirectional electricity meter to track both the power a customer draws from the grid and the excess electricity they export from their onsite renewable system (typically solar) .

When the system produces more electricity than the customer consumes during a given period, the surplus is fed back into the grid, and the customer earns credits, usually at the same retail rate, which are applied against future electricity usage
Fossil fuel subsidies

fossil fuel subsidies, which amounted to $7 trillion in in 2022and expected to rise up to $8.2 trillion by 2030 according to the IMF, pose a serious barrier to the integration of renewable energy into energy mixes (IMF, 2023) .
A phase out of such subsidies would not only reduce carbon emissions by limiting the accessibility of fossil fuels, but by also freeing up funds for other public interventions.

Part 2: Industry Strategies for Scaling Innovations

A key partner in the transition towards a sustainable energy future is the private sector, which plays a critical role not only in funding but also in shaping industrial strategies that accelerate the deployment and adoption of clean energy technologies.

Industries and the private sector are significant energy consumers and innovation drivers. Their active engagement is essential to scale up the production, deployment, and affordability of renewable technologies.
By developing robust industrial ecosystems and targeted innovation strategies, the private sector can reduce costs, diversify supply chains, and expand market opportunities.

Moreover, industry-led innovation supported by enabling government policy can unlock the full potential of emerging technologies, from green hydrogen and battery storage to digital solutions for smart grids and energy efficiency.
Improving Clean Energy Value Chains
One key lever to scale innovation and accelerate just energy transitions, is to secure the value chains that underpin clean energy manufacturing.

A strategic response to these vulnerabilities is to localize and diversify manufacturing, thereby increasing national or regional self-reliance and building industrial capacity.

India’s recent push towards domestic manufacturing of solar modules, exemplifies this strategy, aiming to fully encompass the solar panel value chain.

India’s solar manufacturing capacity is projected to more than double by 2030, with module capacity reaching 160 gigawatts and cell capacity reaching 120 gigawatts, up from 80 gigawatts and 15 gigawatts respectively in 2025 (PV Magazine, 2025).

In addition to localizing manufacturing of clean energy equipment, nations are aiming to secure long-term and sustainable access to the critical and rare earth minerals required to feed this manufacturing process.

A key example of this is the EU’s Critical Raw Minerals Act (agreed in 2023), which seeks to reduce the EU’s dependence on foreign suppliers, by setting benchmarks for domestic capacities to be reached by 2030:

- 10% of the EU's annual needs for extraction;
- 40% for processing
- 25% for recycling
- No more than 65% of EU’s annual needs of each strategic raw material at any relevant stage of processing should come from a single third country.

Similar strategies are being explored notbaly in Africa through regional initiatives to develop battery and solar component industries closer to mineral sources.
Strengthening supply chains is only one part of the equation.
To achieve scale, industries must also accelerate investment flows into clean energy, mobilizing private capital at speed and scale in order to close the energy investment gap.
Private investment is central to scaling up clean energy infrastructure and innovation.
Governments alone cannot finance the transition; industry must step in with both capital and technical expertise.

Accelerating Private Sector Investment in Clean Energy
Private investment is central to scaling up clean energy infrastructure and innovation.
Governments alone cannot finance the transition; industry must step in with both capital and technical expertise.
Innovative financing mechanisms can help de-risk projects and attract private investment into new markets and technologies.
They also help corporations meet their sustainability and net-zero targets.

REN21 finds that corporate PPAs accounted for approximately 10% of global renewable energy capacity additions in 2023, with a record 46 GW of solar and wind contracts signed—up 30% from 2022 (REN21, 2024).
Industrial partnerships for co-development and scale-up of technologies—such as hydrogen, green steel, or carbon capture—are also crucial.
For example, the Mission Possible Partnership brings together companies across heavy industry sectors to coordinate technology pilots and jointly scale decarbonization pathways.
Public-private investment platforms, such as the Just Energy Transition Partnerships (JETPs), are also emerging as blueprints for co-investment, particularly in coal-reliant economies.
These bring together national governments, donors, development banks, and industry to align transition finance with local priorities.

Part 3: Workforce Development and Knowledge Sharing

In addition to policy, and technology from the private sector and industries, successful and inclusive energy transition also largely depends on people, those who will design, build, operate, and benefit from new energy systems.
Investing in human capital and knowledge ecosystems is a foundational pillar of a just and effective energy transition.
This means equipping workers with the right skills, democratizing access to technical expertise, and fostering global collaboration in innovation and implementation.
Building an Inclusive and Future-Ready Energy Workforce
Given the rapid growth of the renewable energy sector, labor market demands are evolving quickly, creating an <strong>urgent need for more specialized workers.
At the same time, the shift from fossil fuels to renewable energy must be managed carefully to avoid reinforcing or creating new social and economic inequalities.
Ensuring that both the current and future workforce are adequately prepared for this transition is essential.

According to a 2019 ILO report, the green economy could generate up to 24 million new jobs by 2030 if the right policies are implemented, although 6 million existing jobs may be at risk of being lost ( ILO, 2018).

Reskilling individuals to prepare them for this transition is crucial in this regard.

To this effect, the EU is implementing their RES-SKILL initiative, which aims to reskill coal workers from 6 EU countries, representing around 81% of the industry, aiming to transition them into in-demand renewable energy jobs.
This effort was conducted through an assessment of complementarities between coal jobs and renewable energy jobs.
This led to the creation of transition profiles, the provision of open learning platforms, and the creation of centers of excellence.
Similar approaches are needed globally, particularly in regions with large fossil fuel employment bases such as India, South Africa, or Indonesia.
Ensuring just transition plans include educational institutions, labor unions, and industry actors is critical to success.
Such initiatives must also address structural inequalities, especially gender disparities.
A 2025 UN Women report reveals that women make up only 32% of the global renewable energy workforce (UN Women, 2025).
Without intentional strategies, the clean energy transition risks replicating the same exclusionary patterns seen in legacy energy sectors.
Technology Sharing

While reskilling and inclusion efforts build the necessary workforce for a sustainable energy future, they must be accompanied by an equally ambitious agenda for knowledge and technology sharing to close the global divide and accelerate impact.
Knowledge Disparity
Developing countries face a stark knowledge and technology gap that, if left unaddressed, could significantly delay a just energy transition and perpetuate existing inequalities.

Today, less than 15 % of global clean energy investment is directed to these nations, even though they represent nearly two-thirds of the world’s population ( WEF, 2025) This financial shortfall is compounded by a significant skills deficit: there were only 324,000 renewable energy jobs in Africa in 2023, compared to 16.2 million globally, largely due to the lack of technical training for engineers and technicians (Reuters, 2024).

Additionally, patent protections and intellectual property regimes often restrict access to crucial technologies developed predominantly in the Global North, making them either too expensive or hard to adapt locally.
Without equitable knowledge transfer developing nations risk being locked into carbon-intensive energy pathways, and missing out on green job creation.
Partnerships for Just Energy Transition

Developing nations who usually perform in similar socio-economic environments can share lessons learned, as well as guidelines for implementation of renewable energy projects in challenging environments.
Through the establishment of regional knowledge hubs, learning can be democratized and processes re-engineered.

Such is the case with the Africa Clean Energy- Technical Assistance Facility, a UK FCDO funded project, which aims to provide market based private sector solutions to renewable energy electrification problems, while promoting the use of standalone solar energy systems.
EU-TAF

A simple example of this is the EU-Technical Assistance Facility, which provides support in technical areas such as feasibility studies, impact assessments, regulatory support, public private partnerships and legal services.
Such initiatives streamline access to expertise and information, while also building a common knowledge base.
Opportunities for the future

In addition, enhanced collaboration between advanced economies, which have the resources to invest in costly early-stage research and development, and developing economies which have the potential to deploy and benefit from these solutions, can enable a more just, equitable, and accelerated energy transition.

Measures such as open licensing, along with joint ventures, targeted financing, and capacity-building initiatives, can play a critical role in facilitating this exchange and unlocking shared progress.

However, these relations can prove to be imbalanced, as Kruckenberg (2015) points out, it remains essential to empower local actors, while also balancing between a science led attitude, and a need-based attitude grounded in local contexts and social complexities.
Partnerships that engage in an “open negotiation of knowledge” stand a better chance of succeeding (Kruckenberg, 2015).
Key Takeaways
If you only have space to remember 3 things:

Identify policy and market mechanisms that drive renewable energy adoption, including Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs), carbon pricing instruments, feed-in tariffs, and the phasing out of fossil fuel subsidies.
Analyze how innovation ecosystems and private sector engagement (through local manufacturing and blended finance) can accelerate clean energy transitions, particularly in developing countries.
Understand the importance of workforce development, equity, and global knowledge exchange in ensuring a just transition, with a focus on reskilling, gender inclusion, and technology transfer.
